title: Rome commonly rejects this: freedom formally in the will alone; free choice the will itself under an aspect
source_text: VII. Verum haec sententia communiter in Schola Romana rejicitur. Nam plerique illius Doctores existimant intellectum non esse formaliter liberum, sed libertatem esse per se & formaliter in sola voluntate. Ac proinde docent liberum arbitrium non esse potentiam a voluntate diversam, nec aliud quam ipsam voluntatem, certo tamen respectu & modo consideratam: ita ut quamvis voluntas & liberum arbitrium sint potentia reapse eadem, nihilominus Liberum Arbitrium a voluntate sit ratione distinctum.
pass_a_gloss: But this opinion is commonly rejected in the Roman School. For most of its Doctors think that the intellect is not formally free, but that liberty is of itself and formally in the will alone. And accordingly they teach that free choice is not a power different from the will, nor anything other than the will itself, yet considered under a certain respect and mode: so that although the will and free choice are really the same power, nevertheless Free Choice is distinguished from the will by reason.
pass_b_english: The Roman School, however, generally rejects this view. Most of its teachers hold that the intellect is not free formally, and that freedom belongs in its own right and formally to the will alone.

So they teach that free choice is no power other than the will. It is simply the will, regarded in a certain respect and manner. The will and free choice are thus one and the same power in reality, yet free choice is distinguished from the will by a distinction of reason.

lemmas.gloss: under a certain respect and mode

choices.why: Kept as in the preceding locus on free choice in general, so the Roman and Reformed accounts are compared in one vocabulary.
